rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication should begin by acknowledging one's weakness, then recall God's abundant favors, as Zachariah does.
rows.anchor: أن المحتسب أن يذكر في مقدمة الدعاء عجز النفس وضعفها كما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication should seek something tied to religion rather than mere worldly benefit.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الدعاء لأجل شيء متعلق بالدين لا لمحض الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A supplicant should address God with the vocative “My Lord,” as Zachariah does here.
rows.anchor: أن يكون الدعاء بلفظ يا رب على ما في هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zachariah's virtues include utter dependence on God, answered prayer, being addressed and given good news, and a tongue restrained from ordinary speech but able to glorify God.
rows.anchor: اعتقال لسانه عن الكلام دون التسبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets may ask God for signs, as Zachariah asks for a sign.
rows.anchor: أنه يجوز للأنبياء عليهم السلام طلب الآيات لقوله رب اجعل لي آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's creation of a child for parents in extreme old age refutes those who attribute natural events to fixed natures.
rows.anchor: كونه تعالى قادرا على خلق الولد وإن كان الأبوان في نهاية الشيخوخة ردا على أهل الطبائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God created Zachariah before when he was nothing is presented as a basis for sound religious inference.
rows.anchor: وقد خلقتك من قبل ولم تك شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi reads the verse as saying the nonexistent is not a thing, but concludes it does not settle the disputed point because a human is not the separately existing atoms that later compose him.
rows.anchor: أن المعدوم ليس بشيء والآية نص في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Maryam account omits when Zachariah prayed; Āl ʿImrān supplies the occasion: seeing Mary receive extraordinary provision prompted his own prayer.
rows.anchor: لما رأى خرق العادة في حق مريم عليها السلام طمع فيه في حق نفسه فدعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl ʿImrān explicitly says the angels announced the news, while Maryam seems to make God the caller; Razi says both may have called, so there is no conflict.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه السورة الأظهر أن المنادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The different order of Zachariah's age and his wife's barrenness is no contradiction, since the conjunction wāw does not require sequence; what reached him, he also reached.
rows.anchor: وجوابه أن الواو لا تقتضي الترتيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three days in Āl ʿImrān and three nights in Maryam mean three complete days with their nights, during which he was sound.
rows.anchor: دلت الآيتان على أن المراد ثلاثة أيام بلياليهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yahya's story precedes Jesus's because a child born to two elderly parents is closer to ordinary experience than one born without a father; teaching proceeds from easier to harder cases.
rows.anchor: خلق الولد من شيخين فانيين أقرب إلى مناهج العادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time clause is an appositional specification of Mary, since an occasion contains what happens in it; the narrative focuses on the time of this remarkable event.
rows.anchor: إذ بدل من مريم بدل اشتمال لأن الأحيان مشتملة على ما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabdh originally means casting or throwing; intibādh derives from it and can mean withdrawing aside, with related uses in the words for foundling, wine, and a sale concluded by casting.
rows.anchor: النبذ أصله الطرح والإلقاء والانتباذ افتعال منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary quickly withdrew from her family to a place toward the east.
rows.anchor: تباعدت وانفردت على سرعة إلى مكان يلي ناحية الشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The screen was more likely a curtain between Mary and her family than a wall or other barrier.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أنها جعلت بين نفسها وبينهم سترا وهذا الوجه الثاني أظهر

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: One explanation is that Mary withdrew during menstruation to await purification, then Gabriel came after she was clean.
rows.anchor: لما رأت الحيض تباعدت عن مكانها المعتاد للعبادة لكي تنتظر الطهر

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Another explanation is that Mary sought privacy so that worship would not distract her.
rows.anchor: أنها طلبت الخلوة لئلا تشتغل عن العبادة

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Another view has her sitting east of the house, screened, to wash after menstruation.
rows.anchor: قعدت في مشرقة للاغتسال من الحيض محتجبة بشيء يسترها

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: A further report says Mary lived in a separate sanctuary room at Zachariah's brother-in-law's house, escaped through an opened roof to the wilderness to comb her hair, and then met the angel.
rows.anchor: كان لها في منزل زوج أختها زكرياء محراب على حدة تسكنه

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Another view says she went into the wilderness because she was thirsty and wanted to draw water.
rows.anchor: عطشت فخرجت إلى المفازة لتستقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All proposed motives for her seclusion are possible, but the wording does not establish which is correct.
rows.anchor: كل هذه الوجوه محتمل وليس في اللفظ ما يدل على ترجيح واحد منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eastern place was east of Jerusalem or of Mary's home; Ibn ʿAbbās links Christians' eastward prayer direction with Jesus's eastern birthplace.
rows.anchor: المكان الشرقي هو الذي يلي شرقي بيت المقدس أو شرقي دارها وعن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the spirit sent to Mary as Gabriel.
rows.anchor: الأكثرون : إنه جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim identifies the spirit as the spirit that took human form in Mary's womb.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم إنه الروح الذي تصور في بطنها بشرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers Gabriel: Gabriel is called Spirit elsewhere, and the later declaration that he is the Lord's messenger who will grant a boy fits him.
rows.anchor: والأول أقرب لأن جبريل عليه السلام يسمى روحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Spirit may reflect his spiritual nature, creation from spirit, reviving religion, or God's affectionate attribution; Abū Ḥaywa's fatḥ reading can evoke the breath and spiritual life promised to the near ones.
rows.anchor: وسمي روحا لأنه روحاني وقيل خلق من الروح وقيل لأن الدين يحيا به

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywa reads rūḥan with fatḥ, connecting Gabriel with the life-breath of worshippers or with the promised spirit of the near ones.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة روحنا بالفتح لأنه سبب لما فيه روح العباد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view says Gabriel appeared as a handsome, beardless young man; another says he looked like Mary's contemporary, a temple servant named Yusuf; the text does not decide between them.
rows.anchor: ظهر لها على صورة شاب أمرد حسن الوجه سوي الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel appeared human so Mary could converse without fear; an angelic appearance might have frightened her and prevented her hearing him.
rows.anchor: وإنما تمثل لها في صورة الإنسان لتستأنس بكلامه ولا تنفر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A first objection says that if angels or jinn can assume a known person's form, one cannot be sure today's observed person is the one seen yesterday, inviting skepticism.
rows.anchor: لا يمكننا القطع بأن هذا الشخص الذي أراه في الحال هو زيد الذي رأيته بالأمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that such doubt also follows from belief in a freely acting Creator able to make an exact duplicate, or from extraordinary planetary conjunctions posited by naturalists.
rows.anchor: ذلك التجويز لازم على الكل لأن من اعترف بافتقار العالم إلى الصانع المختار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second objection asks how Gabriel's enormous body could become human-sized: loss of parts would destroy him, while overlapping parts is impossible.
rows.anchor: ذلك الشخص العظيم كيف صار بدنه في مقدار جثة الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that a bodily Gabriel may have few essential parts and many additional ones, or, if spiritual, may assume large or small forms without difficulty.
rows.anchor: له أجزاء أصلية وأجزاء فاضلة والأجزاء الأصلية قليلة جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third objection says that allowing Gabriel to take human form would also allow forms as small as insects, an absurd result.
rows.anchor: فلم لا يجوز تمثله في صورة جسم أصغر من الآدمي حتى الذباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth objection says assuming forms could undermine mass-transmitted reports, for example by making the person at Badr someone disguised as Muhammad.
rows.anchor: أن تجويزه يفضي إلى القدح في خبر التواتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says reason allows such forms in principle; reliable transmitted revelation establishes that the insect-like and report-undermining possibilities do not occur.
rows.anchor: أصل التجويز قائم في العقل وإنما عرف فساده بدلائل السمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred sense is: if you fear God, invoking Him will protect me from you; Mary knows refuge is effective through a God-fearing person, as in the conditional appeal to believers about usury.
rows.anchor: أرادت أن كان يرجى منك أن تتقي الله ويحصل ذلك بالاستعاذة به فإني عائذة به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation is that she challenges the stranger's piety because he has presumed to look at her and be alone with her.
rows.anchor: ما كنت تقيا حيث استحللت النظر إلي وخلوت بي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation says she mistook him for a notorious womanizer named Taqī; Razi prefers the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: إنسان فاجر اسمه تقى يتبع النساء فظنت مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel's assurance that he is the Lord's messenger would not alone remove Mary's fear; he must have shown a sign she recognized, perhaps based on her knowledge of angels from Zachariah.
rows.anchor: الخوف لا يزول بمجرد هذا القول بل لا بد من دلالة تدل على أنه جبريل

rows.speaker: القاضي عبد الجبار
rows.claim: Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār objects that if Mary was not a prophet and God sent only men, this messenger episode is inexplicable; he answers that it occurred in Zachariah's prophetic era.
rows.anchor: وسأل القاضي عبد الجبار في تفسيره نفسه فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the answer that this was Zachariah's miracle, since a miracle must be known to its prophet and Zachariah knew nothing of these events; it was Mary's honor or a foretoken of Jesus instead.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف لأن المعجز إذا كان مفعولا للنبي فأقل ما فيه أن يكون عليه السلام عالما به

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads li-yahaba with an open yāʾ, making God the giver of the boy.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر ونافع ليهب بياء مفتوحة بعد اللام

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ also reads li-yahaba with an open yāʾ, making God the giver of the boy.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر ونافع ليهب بياء مفتوحة بعد اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining readers use the hamza reading, and the “I grant” wording can attribute the gift to Gabriel as the commanded immediate cause or to his truthful announcement as a gift in effect.
rows.anchor: والباقون بهمزة مفتوحة بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi considers whether Gabriel can assemble matter and create life, reason, and speech; he rejects the premise that every created thing must be spatial or in a spatial subject, or that shared spatiality makes essences alike.
rows.anchor: لا نسلم أن كل محدث إما متحيز أو قائم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even granting that Gabriel is a body, similarity among bodies in occupying space does not entail sameness of essence; God could single some bodies out for powers unavailable to humans.
rows.anchor: الاشتراك في الصفات لا يوجب الاشتراك في ماهيات المواصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the decisive basis for denying Gabriel this creative power is the community's consensus.
rows.anchor: والجواب الحق أن المعتمد في دفع هذا الاحتمال اجماع الأمة فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakī can mean sinless, growing through purification, or pure in the qualities needed for prophethood; Razi rejects combining all meanings because one word cannot bear two senses under his legal-theory principle.
rows.anchor: الزكي يفيد أمورا ثلاثة : الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus is called pure despite owning nothing: his wealth is wisdom and scripture, while worldly observers wrongly equate purity with money and poverty with misery.
rows.anchor: سيرته الفقر وغناه الحكمة والكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary is astonished because ordinary experience requires a man for childbirth, not because she doubts God's power; she knew God created Adam without parents.
rows.anchor: لأنها عرفت بالعادة أن الولادة لا تكون إلا من رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No man touched me” is a euphemism for lawful intercourse, whereas adultery is described plainly; adding “nor was I unchaste” emphasizes the gravest possible suspicion, unlike the shorter Āl ʿImrān wording.
rows.anchor: أنها جعلت المس عبارة عن النكاح الحلال لأنه كناية عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated denial may also intensify the point, like the repeated mention of the middle prayer and naming Gabriel and Michael after angels and messengers generally.
rows.anchor: أن أعادتها لتعظيم حالها كقوله

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf glosses baghiyy as a woman who pursues men; al-Mubarrad derives it as faʿūl from baghwiyy with assimilation, while Ibn Jinnī calls it faʿīl.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) البغي الفاجرة التي تبغي الرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel's answer that this is easy echoes Āl ʿImrān: God creates whatever He wills and needs no tools or materials to originate it.
rows.anchor: لا يمتنع عليه فعل ما يريد خلقه ولا يحتاج في إنشائه إلى الآلات والمواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns in “it is easy for Me” and “to make him a sign” may refer to creating Jesus, or to Jesus himself; “mercy from Us” may modify making him a sign or the sign-and-mercy pair.
rows.anchor: أن تكون راجعة إلى الخلق أي أن خلقه علي هين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A matter decreed” means fixed in God's knowledge and unable to fail, since otherwise His knowledge would become ignorance; all possibilities ultimately terminate in the Necessary Existent, so grief is pointless.
rows.anchor: معلوم لعلم الله تعالى فيمتنع وقوع خلافه لأنه لو لم يقع لانقلب علم الله جهلا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says that knowing God's secret in destiny makes afflictions feel light.
rows.anchor: من عرف سر الله في القدر هانت عليه المصائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran describes God's breathing into Mary and into Adam; Razi notes that the wording concerning Jesus can grammatically refer to Mary because Jesus was in her womb.
rows.anchor: وقال فنفخنا فيها لأن عيسى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One group says God Himself was the breather, citing the wording about breathing His spirit into Jesus and the analogy to Adam.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم كان النفخ من الله تعالى لقوله

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say Gabriel breathed, since “I shall grant you” suggests the pregnancy was caused through his action by God's command.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : النافخ هو جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb's account has Gabriel blow into Mary's collar, with the breath reaching her womb.
rows.anchor: قول وهب إنه نفخ جبريل في جيبها حتى وصلت إلى الرحم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another account places Gabriel's breath in the lower hem, from which it reached the womb.
rows.anchor: في ذيلها فوصلت إلى الفرج

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says Gabriel blew through the sleeve into Mary's chest; Zachariah's wife realized she was pregnant when embracing her and said the child in her womb bowed to Mary's child.
rows.anchor: قول السدي أخذ بكمها فنفخ في جنب درعها فدخلت النفخة صدرها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further view says the breath entered Mary's mouth, reached her belly, and she conceived immediately.
rows.anchor: أن النفخة كانت في فيها فوصلت إلى بطنها فحملت في الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative has an omitted clause: the matter was decreed, Gabriel breathed into Mary, and she conceived.
rows.anchor: إذ عرفت هذا ظهر أن في الكلام حذفا وهو

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Reports put Mary's age at conception at thirteen or twenty and say she had menstruated twice, but the Quran establishes none of these details.
rows.anchor: قيل حملته وهي بنت ثلاث عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “She withdrew with him” means she withdrew while Jesus was inside her, like a plant that grows bearing oil within it.
rows.anchor: أي اعتزلت وهو في بطنها كقوله

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: In a report transmitted by al-Thaʿlabī, Mary's cousin Yusuf the carpenter served the Zion sanctuary with her; noticing her pregnancy, he hesitated to suspect her because of her constant piety.
rows.anchor: عن وهب قال : إن مريم لما حملت بعيسى

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Yusuf asks whether crops, trees, or children can exist without ordinary causes; Mary answers that God first created crops, trees, Adam, and his wife without those causes, and Yusuf's suspicion subsides.
rows.anchor: هل ينبت زرع بغير بذر وهل تنبت شجرة من غير غيث

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: The report says Yusuf took over Mary's sanctuary service when pregnancy weakened her; before birth God told her to leave lest her people kill the child, and Yusuf carried her toward Egypt.
rows.anchor: أخرجي من أرض قومك لئلا يقتلوا ولدك فاحتملها يوسف إلى أرض مصر

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: In the report, Mary reached Egypt in cold weather, went into labor, and was forced to a palm trunk where she delivered.
rows.anchor: أدركها النفاس فألجأها إلى أصل نخلة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other proposed reasons for Mary's withdrawal are embarrassment before Zachariah, shame given her reputation for piety, or fear for the child's safety; Razi says the text chooses none.
rows.anchor: استحيت من زكريا فذهبت إلى مكان بعيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās's first view gives the pregnancy nine months, like other women, arguing that an exceptional duration would have been mentioned among Mary's extraordinary merits.
rows.anchor: قول ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إنها كانت تسعة أشهر كما في سائر النساء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view gives eight months, claiming Jesus was the only child born at eight months to survive.
rows.anchor: أنها كانت ثمانية أشهر

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ holds that Mary's pregnancy lasted seven months.
rows.anchor: قول عطاء وأبي العالية والضحاك سبعة أشهر

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya holds that Mary's pregnancy lasted seven months.
rows.anchor: قول عطاء وأبي العالية والضحاك سبعة أشهر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk holds that Mary's pregnancy lasted seven months.
rows.anchor: قول عطاء وأبي العالية والضحاك سبعة أشهر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other reported durations are six months, or three hours divided among conception, formation, and birth.
rows.anchor: ثلاث ساعات حملته في ساعة وصور في ساعة ووضعته في ساعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās makes the pregnancy one hour; successive fa-conjunctions in the narrative suggest immediate sequence, and al-Suddī says the distant place was the far side of her prayer niche.
rows.anchor: قول ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أيضا كانت مدة الحمل ساعة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “Be, and it is” analogy with Adam in Āl ʿImrān also supports instantaneous conception, since a gestational interval applies to conception from semen.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن عيسى عليه السلام كما قال الله تعالى له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaṣiy means distant; some locate the place at the farthest edge of the home, behind a mountain, or on the journey with her cousin Yusuf.
rows.anchor: أي بعيد من أهلها

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf says ajāʾa is derived from jāʾa but shifted to mean forcing someone to a place; labor drove Mary to the palm trunk.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : { * أجاء } منقول من جاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary may have gone to the palm to hold it for easier labor, to brace herself, or to hide from gossip; Razi connects the last possibility to her wish for death.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل للتقوية والاستناد إليها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, in one transmission, reads al-mikhāḍ with kasra, relating it to the fetus's motion in the womb.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير في رواية المخاض بالكسر يقال مخضت الحامل

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf describes the palm as a famous dry trunk in the winter desert, with no crown, fruit, or greenery; the definite article can identify a locally known tree or the species.
rows.anchor: قال في ( الكشاف ) كان جذع نخلة يابسة في الصحراء

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The palm provides dates especially suited to a postpartum woman; as palms normally fruit only after pollination, God producing dates without it parallels Jesus's birth without a father.
rows.anchor: ليطعمها منها الرطب الذي هو أشد الأشياء موافقة للنفساء

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says exile and the agony of childbirth made Mary forget the angels' good news about Jesus.
rows.anchor: قال وهب : أنساها كربة الغربة وما سمعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous people commonly wish for death during severe trials; Razi cites reports from Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAlī at the Camel, and Bilāl as examples.
rows.anchor: أن عادة الصالحين إذا وقعوا في بلاء أن يقولوا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that Mary wished to die to prevent others from committing the sin of speaking against her, while remaining content with God's promise.
rows.anchor: لعلها قالت ذلك لكي لا تقع المعصية ممن يتكلم فيها

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf explains nasiy as something meant to be discarded and forgotten, like a menstrual cloth; Mary wished to be a negligible thing that people ordinarily forget.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) النسي ما من حقه أن يطرح وينسى

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb reads nasiy with fatḥ; al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza do likewise, while the rest read it with kasr, the two vowels being dialect variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب والأعمش وحمزة نسيا بالفتح

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī reads nasīʾan with hamza, meaning thin milk mixed with water that its family forgets because it is so little.
rows.anchor: وقرأ محمد بن كعب القرظي نسيئا بالهمزة وهو الحليب المخلوط بالماء

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads mansiy with kasr as a vowel-assimilation form, like al-mughayyir and al-minkhar.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش منسيا بالكسر على الإتباع

rows.speaker: زر
rows.claim: The well-known reading is fanādāhā; Zirr and ʿAlqama read fa-khāṭabahā, “he addressed her.”
rows.anchor: قرأ زر وعلقمة فخاطبها

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: For min, Nāfiʿ reads the initial mīm with kasr, while the common reading has fatḥ; Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ also read kasr.
rows.anchor: وكسره وهو قراءة نافع وحمزة والكسائي وحفص

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies the caller as Jesus, as does Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: أنه عيسى عليه السلام وهو قول الحسن وسعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: جبريل
rows.claim: Another view identifies the caller as Gabriel, who attended Mary like a midwife.
rows.anchor: أنه جبريل عليه السلام وأنه كان كالقابلة للولد

rows.speaker: ابن عيينة
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUyayna distinguishes the readings: under kasr the caller is the angel, under fatḥ it is Jesus; ʿĀṣim is also cited for this view.
rows.anchor: وهو مروي عن ابن عيينة وعاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers Jesus: fatḥ suggests someone already known to be below her, namely the child, whereas kasr does not require Gabriel; the place is also unsuitable for an angel because it exposes her private parts.
rows.anchor: بفتح الميم إنما يستعمل إذا كان قد علم قبل ذلك أن تحتها أحدا

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī argues that Mary could signal Jesus as her answer only if she knew he could speak.
rows.anchor: دليل الحسن بن علي عليه السلام أن عيسى عليه السلام لو لم يكن كلمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Jesus called, God made him speak at birth to comfort Mary, remove her loneliness, and show the status Gabriel had promised; if Gabriel called, he was sent to remind her of earlier good news.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى أنه تعالى أنطقه لها حين وضعته تطييبا لقلبها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: If Gabriel is the caller, “from beneath her” may refer to a shared level and a local reference point, so one nearer it is above and one farther below, as al-Kalbī explains for the battle verse.
rows.anchor: وفسر الكلبي قوله تعالى : { إذ جاءوكم من فوقكم

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: If the phrase marks elevation, ʿIkrima reports that Mary gave birth on a raised place; another report has Gabriel call from beneath the palm tree.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا الوجه روي عن عكرمة أنها كانت حين ولدت على مثل رابية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording does not establish whether Mary saw the caller.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون مريم قد رأته وأنها ما رأته وليس في اللفظ ما يدل

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: All commentators except al-Ḥasan and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd take sarī as a stream or channel, named for the water that flows in it; those two identify Jesus as a noble, eminent person.
rows.anchor: اتفق المفسرون إلا الحسن وعبد الرحمن بن زيد أن السري هو النهر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan first interprets sarī as Jesus, a noble man, but a report says he later retracted after Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥumayrī corrected him to “stream.”
rows.anchor: وروي أن الحسن رجع عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stream reading is supported by a prophetic report identifying sarī as a channel and by the instruction to eat and drink.
rows.anchor: أنه سأل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن السري فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who read Jesus argue a stream would be beside Mary, not below her, and invoke the parallel describing Jesus and his mother sheltered at a hill with a spring; Razi answers that “below” can mark relative nearness on level ground.
rows.anchor: أن النهر لا يكون تحتها بل إلى جانبها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: If sarī is water, one view says Gabriel struck the ground with his foot and a fresh stream appeared; another says flowing water was already there.
rows.anchor: أن جبريل عليه السلام ضرب برجله فظهر ماء عذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers the newly created stream because “God has made” indicates a new event and its appearance is a miraculous honor for Mary.
rows.anchor: مشعر بالحدوث في ذلك الوقت

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ use sarī generally for a stream, while al-Akhfash restricts it to a small river.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي عبيدة والفراء أو النهر الصغير على ما هو قول الأخفش

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl defines the palm jidhʿ as its lower trunk below the crown; Quṭrub uses the word for any wooden trunk at a tree's base.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : الجذع من النخلة هو الأسفل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats the bāʾ in bijidhʿ as extra, so the command means “shake the trunk”; Arabic also permits verbs with or without bāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : العرب تقول هزه وهز به

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash parses the phrase as “shake dates toward yourself on the palm trunk.”
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون على معنى هزي إليك رطبا بجذع النخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given the winter setting and a dry palm, the wording implies the trunk became a fruit-bearing palm and produced only fresh dates.
rows.anchor: أنه صار نخلة لقوله بجذع النخلة وأنه ما أثمر إلا الرطب

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf lists nine readings of tasāqaṭ, differing in assimilation or deletion of the second tāʾ, consonant choice, and whether tāʾ refers to the palm or yāʾ to the trunk.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : تساقط فيه تسع قراءات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rutaban can be an accusative of specification or an object depending on the reading; janī means freshly gathered, and Ṭalḥa's jiniyan has kasr by vowel matching.
rows.anchor: رطبا تمييز أو مفعول على حسب القراءة الجني المأخوذ طريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stream and dates provide bodily food and drink and console Mary through two miracles.
rows.anchor: جمعنا لك في السري والرطب فائدتين

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites call the extraordinary stream and dates miracles for Zachariah and other prophets; Razi rejects this because Zachariah did not know Mary's location, so they are Mary's honor or a foretoken of Jesus.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : إنها كانت معجزة لزكريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qāf in wa-qarrī is read with kasr in the Najd dialect; dates precede drinking because postpartum blood loss makes the food more urgently needed.
rows.anchor: قرىء بكسر القاف لغة نجد ونقول قدم الأكل على الشرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear usually hurts the spirit more than hunger hurts the body, illustrated by a hungry sheep that refuses food near a wolf but eats after its leg is broken; Mary's fear was milder because Gabriel had already given good news.
rows.anchor: هذا الخوف كان قليلا لأن بشارة جبريل عليه السلام كانت قد تقدمت

rows.speaker: ابن الرومي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Rūmī, transmitting from Abū ʿAmr, reads tarʾinna with hamza, an accent reflecting interchange between hamza and a weak letter.
rows.anchor: قرأ ترئن بالهمزة ابن الرومي عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣawman means silence; a copy attributed to ʿAbd Allāh and a report from Anas read ṣamtan, while others understand fasting because their fasts prohibited speech, making the vow of silence valid in their law.
rows.anchor: صوما } صمتا وفي مصحف عبد الله

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl says a vow of silence may be valid in Islamic law because avoiding human speech and devoting thought to God's remembrance is worship.
rows.anchor: قال القفال لعله يجوز لأن الاحتراز عن كلام الآدميين وتجريد الفكر لذكر الله تعالى قربة

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl also considers that such a vow may be impermissible because it imposes hardship and self-punishment, like vowing to stand in the sun.
rows.anchor: ولعله لا يجوز لما فيه من التضييق وتعذيب النفس كنذر القيام في الشمس

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A report says Abū Bakr told a woman who had vowed silence that Islam had annulled this practice and she should speak.
rows.anchor: روي أنه دخل أبو بكر على امرأة قد نذرت أنها لا تتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary is told to avoid speaking because Jesus's speech can clear her more powerfully, and because silence prevents an argument with fools; refraining from answering a fool is obligatory.
rows.anchor: كلام عيسى عليه السلام أقوى في إزالة التهمة من كلامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says Mary announced the vow when she saw the people and then gestured, since speaking afterward would contradict the vow; another says she had not yet vowed and told them on arrival, with the general wording limited by context.
rows.anchor: فقال قوم : إنها ما تكلمت معهم بذلك

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says childbirth agony and exile made Mary forget the angels' promises; Jesus's first speech then confirmed them, so she carried him to her people.
rows.anchor: ما كان من كلام الملائكة من البشارة بعيسى عليه السلام فلما كلمها جاءها مصداق ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Yusuf took Mary to a cave for forty days until her postpartum bleeding ended; she then carried Jesus home, and he spoke to her on the way as God's servant and Messiah.
rows.anchor: أن يوسف انتهى بمريم إلى غار فأدخلها فيه أربعين يوما حتى طهرت من النفاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both accounts of how Mary returned with the child are possible, but the Quran does not specify which is correct.
rows.anchor: وهذان الوجهان محتملان وليس في القرآن ما يدل على التعيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farīʾ means remarkable or unprecedented, from splitting leather; it could mean an astonishing event without blame or a grave disgrace, and the ensuing reproach makes the blameworthy reading more likely.
rows.anchor: من فري الجلد يروى أنهم لما رأوها ومعها عيسى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: One interpretation, held by Qatāda, Kaʿb, Ibn Zayd, and al-Mughīra, calls Mary sister of a righteous Israelite Aaron, meaning she resembled him in piety; tens of thousands named Aaron followed that righteous man's funeral.
rows.anchor: قتادة وكعب وابن زيد والمغيرة بن شعبة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says they meant Aaron the prophet; Mary was among his descendants, and “sister” can mean a fellow member of a group, as “brother of Hamdan” does.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما عنوا هرون النبي وكانت من أعقابه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A third interpretation compares Mary to a man publicly known for wickedness, using “sister” figuratively rather than as a family relationship.
rows.anchor: كان رجلا معلنا بالفسق فنسبت إليه بمعنى التشبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers that Aaron was Mary's actual righteous brother: literal kinship is the default, and the rebuke is sharper because her father and mother were also righteous.
rows.anchor: أن الأصل في الكلام الحقيقة

rows.speaker: عمرو بن رجاء التميمي
rows.claim: The common reading has imraʾa suʾ; ʿAmr ibn Rajāʾ al-Tamīmī reads abāka imruʾu suʾ, changing the case endings of father and man.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن رجاء التميمي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Mary's gesture means Jesus will answer; al-Suddī says the people angrily called the gesture more insulting than adultery. A report says the nursing child stopped, faced them, leaned on his left, and pointed; other accounts say he spoke then stayed silent until toddlerhood.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي لما أشارت إليه غضبوا غضبا شديدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account has Zachariah ask Jesus to speak in defense during the Jews' dispute, after which Jesus says he is God's servant.
rows.anchor: إن زكرياء عليه السلام أتاها عند مناظرة اليهود إياها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary may have known Jesus could speak because the caller told her not to grieve and instructed her to remain silent; alternatively, God revealed it to Zachariah or to Mary as an honor.
rows.anchor: فصار ذلك كالتنبيه لها على أن المجيب هو عيسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “how can we speak to one who was in the cradle a child,” kāna most likely means that he was present or existed in the cradle.
rows.anchor: فكان ههنا بمعنى حصل ووجد وهذا هو الأقرب في تأويل هذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The cradle may mean Mary's lap: she wrapped Jesus in cloth and brought him, with no prepared cradle because they had no settled home.
rows.anchor: فقيل هو حجرها لما روى أنها أخذته في خرقة فأتت به قومها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means that people normally expect a child who belongs in a cradle to sleep, not speak.
rows.anchor: كيف نكلم صبيا سبيله أن ينام في المهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus begins by declaring servanthood because speech from a newborn could suggest divinity; explicit servanthood removes that suspicion.
rows.anchor: أن الكلام منه في ذلك الوقت كان سببا للوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Jesus's servanthood declaration is true, he is not God; if false, his power is satanic rather than divine, so either way he is not God.
rows.anchor: فإن كان صادقا في مقاله فقد حصل الغرض وإن كان كاذبا لم تكن القوة قوة إلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus prioritizes removing the charge against God over the charge against his mother; denying divine sonship also clears Mary, since God would not honor a fornicating woman with a child of such rank.
rows.anchor: جعل إزالة التهمة عن الله تعالى أولى من إزالة التهمة عن الأم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says Christian doctrine is incoherent: if God is spatial, bodies are originated; if He is not, the proposed mixture of divinity and humanity like water and wine or fire and coal is impossible.
rows.anchor: اختلطت بالناسوت اختلاط الماء بالخمر وامتزاج النار بالفحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi classifies the remaining Christian explanations as union or indwelling of God or an attribute with Jesus's body or soul, granting him creative power, or adopting him as an honorific son like Abraham as friend.
rows.anchor: إما أن يعتقدوا أن الله أو صفة من صفاته اتحد ببدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Union is impossible: if both entities remain, they are two; if both cease and a third appears, that is replacement, not union; and something nonexistent cannot become identical with what exists.
rows.anchor: فإن كانا موجودين فهما اثنان لا واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indwelling as water in a rose, oil in sesame, or fire in coal requires God to be a body, contrary to the Christians' own agreement that He is not one.
rows.anchor: كون الشيء في غيره ككون ماء الورد في الورد والدهن في السمسم والنار في الفحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indwelling like color in a body requires shared location and so also entails corporeality, which Christians deny of God.
rows.anchor: حصوله في الشيء على مثال حصول اللون في الجسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Indwelling as a relational attribute entails dependence; if God depended on something, He would be contingent and need a cause.
rows.anchor: المعقول من هذه التبعية الاحتياج فلو كان الله تعالى في شيء بهذا المعنى لكان محتاجا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since no coherent meaning of divine indwelling can be established, it cannot be affirmed; theologians also argue its necessity would entail either God's origination or an eternal body as His locus.
rows.anchor: احتج الأصحاب على نفي الحلول مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If necessary indwelling made God dependent on a locus, that would contradict the necessary being's independence.
rows.anchor: لو حل مع وجوب أن يحل لكان محتاجا إلى المحل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God's contingent indwelling were an extra attribute, that attribute's own location would cause regress; it would also make God receive a new accident, whose capacity would have existed eternally, implying eternal events.
rows.anchor: لو كان زائدا على ذاته لكان حلول ذلك الزائد في محله زائدا على ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A defender may say indwelling is necessary only conditional on a locus: no locus existed eternally, but when one exists, indwelling follows; the argument questions whether the alternative necessarily implies God's origination or an eternal locus.
rows.anchor: تقتضي الحلول بشرط وجود المحل ففي الأزل ما وجد المحل فلم يوجد شرط هذا الوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A defender could posit a nonbodily locus such as intellect, soul, or prime matter, so an argument against created bodies would not settle the question.
rows.anchor: لم لا يجوز أن يكون محله ليس بجسم ولكنه يكون عقلا أو نفسا أو هيولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another defense says a cause need not depend on its effect even when they cannot be separated, so God's essence might necessitate its indwelling effect without needing the locus.
rows.anchor: العلة وإن امتنع انفكاكها عن المعلول لكنها لا تكون محتاجة إلى المعلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further defense distinguishes God's essence, which remains independent, from the relational attribute of indwelling, which depends on a locus just as other relational attributes become real only through relation.
rows.anchor: جميع الصفات الإضافية الحاصلة له مثل كونه أولا وآخرا ومقارنا ومؤثرا ومعلوما ومذكورا
